A Structure Built to Stay Testable

The app.js/server.js split, centralized error handling, and other seams that exist so this project can be tested without exotic setup.

A few more shapes recur throughout this codebase, all pulling toward the same goal: keep the pieces testable in isolation, without needing a real server, database, or Redis connection running just to check that a function does the right thing.

app.js builds; server.js runs. app.js builds and exports the Express app, but never calls .listen(). server.js imports that app and is the only file that actually starts it listening.

// Figure 0.5: the split, reduced to its essentials
// app.js
const app = express();
app.use(/* ...middleware, routes... */);
export default app;

// server.js
import app from './app.js';
const httpServer = http.createServer(app);
httpServer.listen(env.PORT, /* ... */);

The payoff shows up in testing: supertest (introduced early, used throughout) can import app.js directly and fire requests at it entirely in-memory, with no port ever bound. Anything that genuinely needs a live connection — Socket.IO needs a real http.Server to attach to, the SLA-job scheduler needs Redis — lives in server.js instead, specifically so a test importing app.js is never forced to have either of those running just to check an HTTP response.

Errors are handled in one place, not scattered through every controller. Every route handler is wrapped in asyncHandler, which forwards a rejected promise to Express's next(err) instead of letting it crash the process — Express only catches thrown errors in synchronous handlers on its own, not rejected promises, so this closes that gap once, centrally, rather than wrapping every controller function in its own try/catch. Every error, from any controller, ends up in one error-handling middleware registered at the bottom of app.js, which decides the response shape once for the whole API.

Validation and response-shaping are functions, not framework hooks. Incoming requests are checked against a Zod schema by a small middleware function (validate({ body: createTicketSchema }), applied per route) — not a BaseRequest class a controller extends. Outgoing responses go through a couple of small helper functions, not a Resource/Transformer class either — the same "plain functions first" reasoning from the previous topic, applied to the two ends of a request instead of the controller layer in the middle.

Nothing here is exotic — Express itself doesn't ask for any of it. It's a set of seams chosen on purpose, so that testing this API never requires more than importing app.js and making a request.
